metaTitle: Sell Alabama Mineral Rights | Fair, Patient Evaluation
metaDescription: Sell your Alabama mineral or royalty rights with a patient, portfolio-minded evaluation grounded in real production history and county activity, no pressure.
heroLead: Alabama mineral ownership is often inherited, often fractional, and often confusing to figure out what it is actually worth. We help you understand it before you decide anything.
intro: Whether your family holds coalbed methane royalty acreage in the Black Warrior basin, an aging conventional interest down in south Alabama's oil fields, or a fractional share of both you inherited without much explanation, the starting point is the same: understand your ownership, understand what it is producing or could produce, and only then decide whether holding, leasing, or selling makes the most sense for your household.
We approach this the way a family office approaches any income-producing or speculative asset in a portfolio, with patient, hedged reasoning rather than a fast pitch.

sections.heading: Two very different plays, one state
paragraphs: Alabama's mineral story splits into two distinct regions. The Black Warrior basin, centered on counties like Tuscaloosa, Fayette, and Walker, has been a legacy coalbed methane producing area for decades, with wells that ramp up production as coal seams are dewatered before settling into a longer decline. South Alabama's conventional fields, including the long-producing Citronelle and Manila areas, follow a different pattern entirely, typically peaking earlier and declining faster.

Knowing which region, and which specific play, your acreage sits in changes almost everything about how the interest should be evaluated, which is why we treat that as step one rather than an afterthought.

sections.heading: For owners who inherited more often than bought
paragraphs: A large share of the mineral interests we evaluate across Alabama passed down through family land, often without a clean paper trail at every generational step. Heirs' property and tenancy-in-common ownership are common realities here, particularly on rural acreage that has stayed in a family for generations without formal probate at each transfer.

If that describes your situation, it does not disqualify you from moving forward, it just means the title work may take a bit longer, and we are used to walking families through what a probate filing or heirship affidavit typically resolves.

sections.heading: A patient, portfolio-minded process
paragraphs: We do not quote a number before reviewing your documents, and we do not push toward a fast signature. Value talk from us is always a range tied to your production history, county activity, and the current commodity environment, because that is the honest way to talk about an asset like this.

Selling is not the only outcome we discuss. If leasing, holding, or selling only a partial interest fits your family better, we will say so plainly rather than steering every conversation toward the largest possible transaction.

sections.heading: What to expect when you reach out
paragraphs: You do not need a complete file of documents to start a conversation. A rough sense of the county, whether the interest is producing, and any lease or statement you can find is enough for us to tell you what else, if anything, would help sharpen an evaluation. Owners with fully organized records and owners starting from a single old envelope both go through the same process from that point forward.

From there, we walk through what a fair range looks like and why, and you decide the pace. Some families move quickly. Others want to sit with the numbers for a while, talk to a CPA, or compare against another source, and all of that is completely fine with us.

sections.heading: Guides worth reading before you decide anything
paragraphs: Whether you are trying to make sense of a royalty statement, wondering what documents a sale actually requires, or trying to understand the difference between leasing and selling for your specific situation, our library of guides walks through each of these in plain language, written specifically with Alabama's producing regions in mind rather than generic national content.
None of it requires you to reach out first. Read what is useful, skip what is not, and come to a conversation with whatever questions remain.

faqs.question: Do I have to sell my whole interest?
faqs.answer: No. Many owners sell a portion or retain an override while selling the mineral fee. We will discuss what structure fits your situation rather than assuming a full sale is the only option.

faqs.question: What if I inherited my minerals and the estate was never probated?
faqs.answer: This is common in Alabama and usually resolvable with a probate filing or heirship affidavit. We can point you toward what is typically needed for your specific county.

faqs.question: Is my interest worth anything if it has never been leased?
faqs.answer: Often yes, though the value reflects nearby activity and development potential rather than existing production. We evaluate unleased acreage differently than producing royalty interests.

faqs.question: Will I owe taxes if I sell?
faqs.answer: Likely a capital gains tax on some portion of the sale, though a stepped-up basis for inherited interests often reduces this meaningfully. Talk to your CPA about your specific situation before closing.

faqs.question: Is there any pressure or obligation if I reach out?
faqs.answer: No. Requesting an evaluation is free and does not commit you to selling. Take the information at your own pace.

faqs.question: What if I only know roughly where in Alabama my family's minerals are located?
faqs.answer: That is a fine starting point. Even a general area or family name tied to old land is often enough for us to help you narrow down the county and start locating records.
